blocks.text: A function is a relation with one extra rule bolted on, and that single extra rule turns out to be one of the most consequential constraints in all of mathematics. Where a relation can connect an input to any number of outputs, including zero or several, a function insists that every input connects to exactly one output. This tiny restriction is what makes a function predictable and computable, and it is precisely the structure that every layer of a neural network, every loss computation, and every activation function is built from. Understanding functions precisely, not just as "a formula," is what makes the rest of the AI mathematics stack click into place.

blocks.alt: A function as a relation where each input has exactly one output
blocks.caption: Injective, surjective, and composed functions, the building blocks of a neural network

1. A Function as a Special Kind of Relation

A function f from a set A to a set B is a relation from A to B with one added requirement: for every element a in A, there is exactly one pair (a, b) in the relation, no more and no fewer. This is usually written f(a) equals b, and it is read as "f maps a to b" or "f of a equals b."

The word "exactly" is doing the real work here. A relation is allowed to connect one input to zero outputs, one output, or many outputs; a function forbids the zero case, since every input must have a value, and forbids the many case, since an input cannot have two different outputs at the same time. A relation that connects a single input to two different outputs is not a function, even though it is a perfectly valid relation.

blocks.title: A quick test
blocks.content: To check whether a relation is a function, scan for any input value that appears twice paired with two different outputs. If one exists, it is not a function; otherwise, and provided every input has at least one output, it is.

blocks.text: 2. Domain, Codomain, and Range

The domain of a function is the full set of allowed inputs, every element of A that the function is defined for. The codomain is the set B that outputs are declared to land in, the "target" set announced up front. The range, sometimes called the image, is the actual set of outputs the function produces, which is always a subset of the codomain but does not have to be the whole thing.

This distinction between codomain and range trips people up constantly. A function from the integers to the integers defined by f(x) equals x squared has the integers as its codomain, since that is the declared target set, but its range is only the non-negative perfect squares, since a negative number can never be produced by squaring an integer.

blocks.text: 3. Function Notation and Evaluation

The notation f colon A arrow B declares that f is a function from A to B, and f(a) denotes the specific output produced when the function is evaluated at the specific input a. This notation cleanly separates the definition of a function, which describes the rule in general, from its evaluation, which applies that rule to one particular value.

In code, a function definition and a function call mirror this distinction exactly: defining "def f(x): return x ** 2" declares the rule once, while calling "f(3)" evaluates it at the specific input 3 to produce the single output 9. Every time f is called with the same input, it must return the same output, which is the computational face of the "exactly one output per input" requirement from section 1.

code.content:
def f(x):
    return x ** 2

print(f(3))   # 9, evaluating f at the specific input 3
print(f(3))   # 9 again, must always match: same input, same output
print(f(-3))  # 9 as well, a different input can still land on the same output

blocks.text: 4. Injective Functions

A function is injective, also called one-to-one, if different inputs always produce different outputs; equivalently, no two distinct elements of the domain ever map to the same element of the codomain. Injectivity is a statement about the inputs never colliding on their way to the output side.

f(x) equals x squared over the real numbers is not injective, since f(2) and f(negative 2) both equal 4, two different inputs landing on the same output. Restricting the domain to only non-negative real numbers fixes this: over that smaller domain, no two distinct non-negative numbers square to the same value, so the restricted function is injective.

code.content:
def is_injective(pairs: list) -> bool:
    outputs = [b for (a, b) in pairs]
    return len(outputs) == len(set(outputs))

not_injective = [(2, 4), (-2, 4), (3, 9)]
print(is_injective(not_injective))  # False, both 2 and -2 map to 4

injective_on_nonneg = [(0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 4), (3, 9)]
print(is_injective(injective_on_nonneg))  # True

blocks.text: 5. Surjective Functions

A function is surjective, also called onto, if every element of the codomain is actually hit by the function, meaning the range equals the entire codomain rather than just some subset of it. Surjectivity is a statement about the output side being fully covered, with no element left unreachable.

f(x) equals x squared, declared as a function from the reals to the reals, is not surjective, since negative numbers in the codomain are never produced as an output; the range is only the non-negative reals, a strict subset of the declared codomain. If the codomain is instead declared to be only the non-negative reals, matching the actual range exactly, the same rule becomes surjective.
6. Bijective Functions

A function that is both injective and surjective is called bijective. A bijection pairs up every element of the domain with a unique element of the codomain, with nothing left over on either side: no two inputs share an output, and every possible output is used exactly once.

Bijections are exactly the functions that can be perfectly reversed: because every output came from exactly one input, running the mapping backward from output to input is itself a well defined function, called the inverse. This is why a bijection is sometimes described as a "perfect pairing" between two sets, and why the two sets in a bijection must have the same cardinality when both are finite.

blocks.text: 7. Composition of Functions

Given a function f from A to B and a function g from B to C, the composition of g and f, written g of f, is the function from A to C obtained by first applying f, then feeding its output into g. Formally, (g of f)(a) equals g(f(a)): apply the inner function first, then the outer one.

Composition is how simple functions build up into more complex behavior without ever leaving the world of "one output per input." As long as each individual function respects that rule, the composition automatically respects it too, since feeding one well defined output into another function that itself produces one output per input can never introduce ambiguity.
7.1 Order Matters

Composition is generally not commutative: g of f and f of g usually produce different functions entirely. With f(x) equals x plus 1 and g(x) equals x squared, g of f gives (x plus 1) squared, while f of g gives x squared plus 1; these are different functions, as evaluating both at x equals 2 confirms, giving 9 versus 5.
8. Properties of Composition

Composition is associative: composing three functions f, g, and h, in the sense (h of g) of f, always produces the exact same overall function as h of (g of f), so parentheses can be dropped entirely when composing a chain of functions, and it is written simply as h of g of f.

Every set A has an identity function, written id, defined by id(a) equals a for every a, which changes nothing at all. Composing any function f with the identity function on either side leaves f completely unchanged: f of id equals f, and id of f equals f. The identity function plays the same role for composition that the number 1 plays for multiplication.
9. Inverse Functions

If f is a bijective function from A to B, its inverse, written f with a superscript negative one, is the function from B to A that undoes it exactly: f inverse of f(a) equals a for every a in A, and f of f inverse of b equals b for every b in B. Composing a bijection with its inverse, in either order, always yields the identity function.

Only bijective functions have a true inverse defined over their entire codomain. If a function is not injective, undoing it is ambiguous, since multiple inputs mapped to the same output, so there is no single correct input to return to. If a function is not surjective, some elements of the codomain have no input at all to send them back to, leaving the inverse undefined there.
10. Functions as First Class Objects in Python

In Python, functions are first class objects: they can be assigned to variables, stored in data structures, passed as arguments to other functions, and returned as the result of another function, exactly the way any other value can be. The compose function written in section 7 is itself an example: it takes two functions as input and returns a brand new function as output.

items: A function can be assigned to a variable: g = f, after which calling g(x) behaves identically to calling f(x).
A function can be stored in a list or dictionary, such as {"square": lambda x: x ** 2, "cube": lambda x: x ** 3}.
A function can be passed as an argument to another function, as with map(f, some_list) or sorted(data, key=some_function).
A function can be returned from another function, which is exactly what building a composition or a customized transformation function looks like in practice.

blocks.title: Higher-order functions
blocks.content: A function that takes another function as an argument, or returns one, such as compose from section 7, is called a higher order function. Map, filter, and sorted with a key argument are all standard library higher order functions built on exactly this idea.

blocks.text: 11. AI Relevance: A Neural Network Layer Is a Function

A single layer of a neural network is, precisely, a mathematical function: given an input vector, it deterministically produces exactly one output vector, by applying a fixed set of weights, a bias, and an activation function. Nothing about that description differs from the formal definition of a function given in section 1; the domain is the space of possible input vectors, the codomain is the space of possible output vectors, and the layer is the rule mapping one to the other.

This matters practically because it means every property covered in this lesson applies directly. A layer that is not injective is throwing away information, mapping distinct inputs to the same internal representation, which can be a deliberate design choice, such as pooling, or an unwanted bottleneck. Whether a layers effective range covers its full codomain affects how much of the next layers input space actually gets used.

This function-based framing also explains why the shapes of a layers input and output vectors matter so precisely: the domain and codomain of the layer function are fixed the moment the weight matrix dimensions are chosen, and feeding in a vector of the wrong dimension is exactly analogous to calling a function with an input that does not belong to its declared domain.
12. AI Relevance: A Neural Network Is a Composed Function

A full neural network with several layers is nothing more than a composition of functions, exactly as defined in section 7: if layer one is the function f1, layer two is f2, and layer three is f3, the whole networks output is f3 of f2 of f1 applied to the input, one function feeding directly into the next. Forward propagation, the step of computing a prediction from an input, is literally evaluating this composed function.

This is precisely why activation functions matter so much: if every layer were a purely linear function, the composition of any number of linear functions is still just another linear function, meaning a network with a hundred layers would collapse to the same expressive power as a network with one layer. Inserting a non-linear activation function, such as ReLU or sigmoid, between the linear layers breaks this collapse, which is what allows depth to actually add expressive power rather than being wasted.

blocks.title: Backpropagation and composition
blocks.content: Training a network relies on the chain rule from calculus to differentiate this exact composition of functions with respect to the weights; the composed-function structure of a network is not just a conceptual analogy, it is the literal mathematical object that gradient computation operates on.

blocks.text: 12.1 Depth as Repeated Composition

Adding a layer to a network is, structurally, nothing more than composing one more function onto the existing chain. This is why network depth is often described as how many times the input has been passed through a non-linear transformation, since that is a literal, not just metaphorical, description of repeated function composition.
13. Worked Example

Let f be the function from the integers to the integers defined by f(x) equals 2x, and let g be the function from the integers to the integers defined by g(x) equals x plus 3. Determine whether f is injective and whether it is surjective, then compute the composition g of f and f of g as explicit formulas, and evaluate both at x equals 4 to confirm they differ.

code.content:
def f(x):
    return 2 * x

def g(x):
    return x + 3

# Injectivity: f(a) = f(b) implies 2a = 2b implies a = b, so f is injective.
# Surjectivity: over the integers, f only ever produces even integers,
# so odd targets like 5 are never reached; f is NOT surjective over the integers.

g_after_f = lambda x: g(f(x))   # g(f(x)) = 2x + 3
f_after_g = lambda x: f(g(x))   # f(g(x)) = 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6

print(g_after_f(4))  # 2*4 + 3 = 11
print(f_after_g(4))  # 2*(4+3) = 14, confirming order changes the result

blocks.text: The two compositions differ by a constant, 3 versus 6, which traces directly back to whether the plus-3 step happens before or after the doubling step; this small algebra example is exactly the same order sensitivity that makes the layer ordering inside a neural network architecture meaningful rather than arbitrary.
14. Common Mistakes

items: Confusing the codomain with the range, and assuming every declared output value is actually produced by the function.

Assuming a formula that looks "one-to-one-ish," such as x squared, is automatically injective without checking the full domain; x squared is only injective once the domain is restricted to non-negative numbers.
Treating composition as commutative and assuming g of f equals f of g; the two are generally different functions, as the worked example shows.
Assuming every function has an inverse; only bijective functions have a true inverse defined across the whole codomain.
Forgetting that a relation failing the "exactly one output per input" rule is not a function at all, no matter how natural or common-sense the relation seems.

blocks.text: A reliable habit that avoids most of these mistakes is to explicitly write down the domain, codomain, and rule for a function before asking any question about injectivity, surjectivity, or invertibility, since all three properties are meaningless without a clearly fixed domain and codomain to check them against.

Key Takeaway

A function is a relation with one crucial extra constraint: every input maps to exactly one output. Injective, surjective, and bijective describe increasingly strict ways that mapping can behave, and composition, the act of feeding one functions output into another, is how simple functions combine into arbitrarily complex behavior while still respecting that one-output-per-input guarantee at every step.

This is not an abstract detour: a neural network layer is a function in the exact formal sense defined here, and a full network is a long composition of such functions, with non-linear activation functions inserted precisely to stop that composition from collapsing back down to something no more powerful than a single layer. Every subsequent lesson that touches neural network mechanics is, underneath, still just talking about functions and their composition.
